t.limpinwood nature reserve@-28.3,153.2:
Twenty-odd million years ago, a huge shield volcano stood where the Tweed valley is now, on what became the border between New South Wales and Queensland. Erosion has since carved out its centre, leaving one of the largest erosion calderas in the world, a vast bowl of green farmland ringed by cliffs and ridges, with the volcano's old central plug, Wollumbin, also known as Mount Warning, standing in the middle. Limpinwood Nature Reserve, on the northern rim of the caldera, protects a stretch of subtropical rainforest that is part of the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia, a UNESCO World Heritage Site preserving forests whose lineage goes back to the ancient supercontinent.

The forest is dense and lush, with strangler figs, palms, tree ferns and towering brush box trees. It is home to rare birds such as Albert's lyrebird, a master mimic that can imitate the songs of other birds, and the Coxen's fig parrot, as well as pademelons, small wallabies that feed at the forest edge at dusk. Wollumbin has deep cultural significance for the Bundjalung people, and the summit track is closed to climbers out of respect and for safety.

The riding here is some of the best in the region. The roads that wind through the Tweed valley and up into the ranges, such as the road to Tyalgum and the route through the Numinbah valley into Queensland, are full of tight curves and steep climbs, with views of the caldera and the cliffs. The surface can be rough in places, and landslides sometimes close roads after heavy rain, which can be intense in summer. Watch for wildlife on the roads, especially at dawn and dusk, and cattle on unfenced sections.

Murwillumbah, about twenty-one kilometres away, is a country town of seven thousand with fuel, supermarkets and a good regional art gallery. Smaller villages like Tyalgum and Uki have cafés, pubs and general stores, often with good coffee and local produce. The area grows macadamias, avocados and tropical fruit, so look for roadside stalls. Carry water and sunscreen, and be ready for sudden storms in the afternoon during the wet season.
t.gambubal state forest@-28.2,152.4:
Gambubal State Forest clings to the western side of the Great Dividing Range in southern Queensland, close to the New South Wales border, in country that drops from rainforest-clad ridges down to the grazing land around Killarney and Warwick. The forest adjoins Main Range National Park and belongs to the wider belt of subtropical and temperate rainforest protected as part of the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia. Hoop pine, ancient Antarctic beech on the highest ridges, tree ferns and strangler figs give it a feel of deep time, and it is one of the cooler corners of Queensland in summer.

The roads in this area are a joy for anyone who likes variety. From Killarney, the road to Queen Mary Falls climbs onto the range with tight bends, steep grades and a few rough patches, and the falls themselves, where a creek drops off the escarpment into a gorge, are a classic short stop. The Condamine River Road west of Killarney is famous for its many creek crossings through the gorge, which are fun in the dry and genuinely dangerous after rain, so check conditions and do not push through running water. Forestry tracks inside Gambubal are mostly gravel and can be closed for logging or weather.

Wildlife is everywhere. Look for wallabies at dawn and dusk, which is also when they jump out in front of bikes, so slow down in the half-light. Lyrebirds, whipbirds and king parrots fill the forest with noise, and in spring the gullies smell of damp earth and flowering shrubs. Winter mornings can be frosty on the tops, a surprise in Queensland.

Warwick, around thirty kilometres away, is the main town, a sandstone-built farming centre on the Condamine known for its annual rodeo and its rose gardens, and it is the dependable place for fuel, supplies and a decent meal. Killarney is closer and smaller, with a pub and basic services; do not leave it with a low tank if you plan to explore the range. Carry water, tell someone your route if you go onto the forestry tracks, and allow time to sit by a creek and listen.
t.mount barney national park@-28.3,152.7:
Mount Barney looks like it was put there to be argued about. The rugged double summit rises to around 1,350 metres, the second-highest peak in south-east Queensland, and its bare rhyolite crags stand out above the softer farmland of the Scenic Rim like a fortress somebody forgot to finish. Geologists will tell you it is the eroded core of an ancient volcanic system; locals will tell you it has humbled plenty of overconfident walkers. Either way, it is part of the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia World Heritage area, which stretches along the border ranges between Queensland and New South Wales.

For a rider, the park is something to circle and admire rather than enter. Access is from the Rathdowney side and the Upper Logan roads, through cattle country where the lanes are narrow, the bitumen is sometimes patched and the creek crossings can flood after heavy rain. Cattle grids, wandering stock, kangaroos at dusk and the odd timber truck are your traffic. The Mount Lindesay Highway, the main road toward the border, has some good flowing sections, but the real pleasure is on the minor roads that fan out toward the ranges.

There are no services in the park itself. Rathdowney is a small village with the basics, and Beaudesert, a bit further north, is the place for a full tank, groceries and a proper choice of coffee. Boonah and Kooralbyn are closer as the crow flies but need a longer loop by road, so plan your fuel stops with care before heading out.

The landscape shifts as you climb from the valleys: open eucalypt woodland, grass trees on the dry slopes and pockets of rainforest in the gullies where creeks keep things damp. Bell miners ping in the trees near water, wallabies graze the paddock edges, and in spring the wattles turn whole hillsides yellow. The Logan River starts in these ranges as a clear little stream before it grows into something much larger downstream.

Autumn and winter are the kindest seasons here, with dry, clear days and cool mornings. Summer brings heat, humidity and spectacular afternoon storms that can turn a dirt shoulder into soup in minutes. Pull over somewhere along Upper Logan Road with the mountain filling your mirror and give it a moment; it is one of those shapes you remember long after the ride.
t.mount chinghee national park@-28.3,152.9:
Mount Chinghee is one of those small national parks that most people drive past without noticing, which is a shame, because it guards a beautiful pocket of the border ranges. It lies near the head of the Albert River valley south of Beaudesert, close to the Queensland and New South Wales border, and like its neighbours it forms part of the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia World Heritage area. The trees here are the same subtropical rainforest types that once covered much of the old southern supercontinent, hanging on in the wetter folds of the ranges.

The road that brings riders here is the real attraction. From Rathdowney the Lions Road climbs south toward Kyogle, crossing the range near the famous Border Loop, where the Sydney to Brisbane railway spirals round on itself to gain height. The Lions Road was built by local Lions Club volunteers in the 1970s to link the two valleys, and it shows its character: narrow, twisting, sometimes single lane, with steep pinches, loose gravel on the edges and the odd one-lane bridge. Ride it at a relaxed pace and give oncoming traffic plenty of room on blind corners.

There are no services in the park. For fuel and supplies, Beaudesert to the north and Kyogle to the south are your best bets, each around thirty-five kilometres away. Rathdowney has a small store and pub for a quick stop, but do not count on long hours or wide choice.

The forest is dense and damp, with strangler figs, tall flooded gums on the edges, ferns and moss on the shady banks. Bird calls fill the air: whipbirds cracking their sharp call, lyrebirds mimicking everything they hear, catbirds sounding like disgruntled cats. After rain the creeks run clear and fast over rock, and leeches lie in wait for anyone who wanders into the wet undergrowth in sandals.

Weather in the ranges is changeable. Winter is cool and usually dry, with crisp clear mornings, while summer can bring heavy afternoon storms and humid, sticky air. Plan your ride for the cooler part of the day, and enjoy the feeling of slipping from cattle country into ancient rainforest within a single bend.
t.palen creek state forest@-28.3,152.8:
State forests in Queensland do not always sound romantic, but Palen Creek earns a second look. It sits in the hills south of Rathdowney in the Scenic Rim, between the Logan River country and the border ranges, a mix of eucalypt forest, old timber land and gullies of rainforest that run up toward the New South Wales border. The Gondwana Rainforests of Australia, which are listed by UNESCO, begin a few ridges away, and the wildlife does not care much about the boundary.

The approach is along the Mount Lindesay Highway, the main road between Beaudesert and the border at Woodenbong, and it is a good one. South of Rathdowney the road starts to twist as it climbs toward the range, with open views across cattle paddocks and up to the flat-topped bulk of Mount Lindesay, an old volcanic plug that marks the border. The surface is generally sound but it can be patched, and log trucks and caravans are common enough that you need to read the road ahead and pick your overtakes carefully.

There is nothing in the forest itself beyond tracks and gates. Rathdowney is the nearest stop, small but useful for a drink and a snack, and Beaudesert, about thirty-seven kilometres north, is the market town where you can fill up, find a supermarket and choose between several places for lunch. Kooralbyn is closer on paper but needs a detour.

The forest is a good place to understand how fire and water shape this country. Ridges carry dry eucalypt woodland, blackened trunks showing past burns, grass trees with their spiky skirts, while the gullies hold dark green rainforest where the creeks run. Kookaburras, wedge-tailed eagles circling over the ridges and wallabies browsing the clearings are all common sights. In late winter the wattles flower, and in early summer the cicadas can be deafening.

Choose cool, dry months for the best riding and the clearest views. In the wet, the gravel tracks in the forest turn greasy and creek crossings rise quickly, so stick to the bitumen unless you know what you are doing. Pause at a gate with the engine off, and listen to the bush ticking in the heat; it is a quieter, older kind of Queensland.
t.lamington national park@-28.1,153.1:
Ask anyone in Brisbane about Lamington and they will probably mention one of two roads, and both of them will make you work. The national park covers the high plateau of the McPherson Range on the Queensland side of the border, a huge expanse of rainforest, waterfalls and cliff-edged lookouts at the heart of the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia World Heritage area. It was named after Lord Lamington, a governor of Queensland at the end of the nineteenth century, who is said to have been less than thrilled to have a park, and later a cake, named after him.

The road up to the Green Mountains section from Canungra is the famous one: narrow, steep and wildly twisty, climbing through farmland and then forest with tight hairpins, blind crests and stretches where it narrows to barely more than one lane. The surface is mostly sealed but can be wet, mossy or scattered with leaves, and cars coming down tend to cut corners. Take it slowly and treat every bend as if a bus might be coming round it. The Binna Burra side, reached from Nerang and Beechmont, has its own share of curves and some fine ridge-top views.

Canungra is the natural stop at the foot of the climb: a small town with fuel, cafés and pubs, and the home of a well-known army training centre. For a full range of services, Beaudesert is about twenty kilometres away. Up on the plateau you will find visitor facilities and places to eat near the main walking areas, but do not count on fuel.

The forest itself is extraordinary. Ancient Antarctic beech trees grow on the higher ridges, some of them thousands of years old through their regrowing root systems, and the walking tracks lead past waterfalls and lookouts over the border ranges. Crimson rosellas and king parrots are bold enough to land on your helmet. Lamington is also linked to a famous rescue: in 1937, Bernard O'Reilly found survivors of a crashed Stinson airliner in the forest after others had given up the search.

Come in the cooler months, when the air is crisp and the views stretch far, and avoid weekends if you can. Summer storms can be fierce. Either way, expect the ride down to feel even tighter than the ride up.
t.burnett creek state forest@-28.2,152.6:
In the Scenic Rim, southwest of Brisbane, Burnett Creek runs down from the slopes of the Main Range toward the farmland around Boonah, and the state forest that bears its name covers a stretch of steep, wooded hills where eucalypt forest gives way, in the moister gullies, to subtropical rainforest. This is the edge of the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia, a UNESCO-listed collection of rainforest reserves along the Great Dividing Range in Queensland and New South Wales, including the Border Ranges and the Main Range national parks. The rainforests here are remnants of the forests that covered the ancient supercontinent of Gondwana, and they shelter plants and animals with lineages going back tens of millions of years.

The landscape around Burnett Creek is a mix of cattle country, small farms and forest, with the volcanic peaks of Mount Barney and Mount Maroon rising dramatically to the south. The area is rich in wildlife: kangaroos and wallabies graze at the forest edge, koalas live in the gum trees, and the birdlife is spectacular, from king parrots and lyrebirds to kookaburras laughing at dawn. Settlement came in the nineteenth century, with timber cutters and cattle farmers moving into the valleys, and some old homesteads and timber bridges remain.

The roads in the Scenic Rim are among the best motorcycle routes in southeast Queensland. From Boonah, roads lead west and south through farmland toward the mountains, with good surfaces, light traffic and plenty of curves. The road up to Carneys Creek and the Head, and over the range toward Killarney, offers tight bends, steep gradients and spectacular views. Further roads near the border can be narrow and sometimes gravel. Watch out for wildlife, especially kangaroos at dawn and dusk, and for cattle on unfenced stretches. Summer is hot and humid with storms; autumn and winter are cool and clear, ideal for riding.

There are no services in the forest. Boonah, about thirty kilometres away, is the nearest town, with fuel, cafés, a pub and shops, and Kalbar and Rathdowney offer smaller options. Carry water and snacks, because distances are longer than they look on the map. Pull over at a lookout or by a creek, listen to the birds, and enjoy the mountain air. It is a gorgeous corner of Queensland, and the riding is the kind you remember.
t.amaroo flora reserve@-28.4,153.2:
Behind the coast of northern New South Wales, the Tweed valley sits inside the remains of an enormous shield volcano that erupted some twenty-odd million years ago. Erosion has carved away the centre, leaving a huge caldera, one of the largest in the world, with the steep, forested walls of the Border Ranges and the McPherson Range curving around it and the volcanic plug of Wollumbin, also known as Mount Warning, rising in the middle. The Amaroo Flora Reserve lies on the slopes of this landscape, part of the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia, a UNESCO site of scattered reserves along the Great Dividing Range.

The rainforests here are living relics of the vegetation that covered the supercontinent of Gondwana, with ancient lineages of ferns, conifers and flowering plants, and a remarkable diversity of birds, frogs, possums and other animals. Walking into the forest, with strangler figs, palms and vines all around and the sound of whipbirds and bellbirds, you step into a world that has changed little over millions of years. Wollumbin is a sacred place for the Bundjalung people, the traditional owners, and the summit track is closed out of respect.

For riders, the Tweed valley offers a variety of good roads. From Murwillumbah, roads run through sugar cane fields and banana plantations, along the Tweed river and up into the hills, with tight curves, steep climbs and views of the caldera. The road to Uki, Nimbin and on to Kyogle winds through green hills and valleys, while the roads up into the ranges are narrower and sometimes unsealed. Watch out for wildlife at dawn and dusk, slippery surfaces after rain, and logging trucks on some roads.

Nimbin, about twenty-four kilometres away, is famous for its alternative culture, dating back to the Aquarius Festival of 1973, and its colourful main street is a lively, eccentric place. Murwillumbah, a town of around seven thousand people seventeen kilometres away, has fuel, shops and cafés, and an excellent regional art gallery. The coast, with the beaches of Kingscliff and the Gold Coast to the north, is half an hour away.

The best time to ride is from autumn to spring, when temperatures are mild; summers are hot and humid, with heavy rain and storms. Stop for a coffee and a slice of cake in a café in one of the hinterland villages, and enjoy the view of Wollumbin rising above the green valley.
t.mount clunie flora reserve@-28.3,152.5:
On the border between New South Wales and Queensland, the McPherson Range rises steeply from the farmland, its forested slopes and cliffs marking the rim of an ancient volcanic landscape. Mount Clunie Flora Reserve protects a patch of rainforest on these slopes near Woodenbong, part of the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia, a UNESCO site that preserves some of the oldest rainforests on earth. Here, in the cool upland forest, hoop pines and towering eucalypts mix with rainforest trees, and the forest floor is dense with ferns and mosses.

This is remote country. The nearest towns are small, and the reserve has no visitor facilities, but the surrounding area offers excellent walks in the national parks of the Border Ranges and Main Range. The forest is home to rare birds such as the Albert's lyrebird, famous for its mimicry, and the Coxen's fig-parrot, as well as possums, gliders and frogs.

The riding in this area is superb. The Mount Lindesay Highway, which runs from Brisbane south over the range to Woodenbong and on to Tenterfield, is a favourite with riders, with tight curves through the forest as it crosses the border near Mount Lindesay, a dramatic volcanic peak. Other roads through the area, such as those around Rathdowney, Boonah and Killarney, wind through valleys, over passes and past dairy farms and cattle stations, with views of the ranges. Some roads are unsealed, and surfaces can be rough, so ride with care. Watch out for kangaroos and wallabies at dawn and dusk, cattle on the road, and logging trucks.

To the north, the Scenic Rim region of Queensland offers more wonderful riding, with the peaks of Mount Barney, Mount Maroon and the Main Range rising above the farmland, and small towns like Boonah and Rathdowney offering cafés and pubs where riders gather on weekends.

Boonah, about thirty-seven kilometres away, is the nearest town with a full range of services, including fuel; Woodenbong and Rathdowney have more limited facilities. Carry water, as distances between services can be long. The best time to ride is from autumn to spring; summers can be hot, with storms and heavy rain. Stop at a country pub for a meal and a cold drink, and enjoy the friendly atmosphere and the stories of other riders. A ride through the forests of the range, with the smell of eucalyptus in the air and the call of bellbirds in the trees, is one of the great pleasures of riding in Australia.
t.main range national park@-27.9,152.3:
The Main Range is the wall behind the Scenic Rim, a long line of old volcanic cliffs and ridges that runs along the border between south-east Queensland and New South Wales. It is what remains of a huge volcano that erupted more than twenty million years ago, and the rocks have been eroded into steep escarpments, gorges and waterfalls, with the high points, such as Mount Superbus, reaching nearly fourteen hundred metres. The national park protects dry eucalypt forest on the lower slopes and cool, damp rainforest higher up, with ancient Antarctic beech trees and giant tree ferns that belong to the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia, listed by UNESCO in 1986.

The wildlife is generous. Koalas, wallabies, pademelons, brush turkeys and lyrebirds live here, and early in the morning you may see kangaroos grazing at the edge of the forest. Walking tracks lead to lookouts and waterfalls, and the air smells of eucalyptus and wet leaves.

For riders, the main attraction is Cunningham's Gap, the pass through the range that carries the Cunningham Highway between Brisbane and the inland plains. It was found by the explorer Allan Cunningham in 1828, and still has a thrilling sequence of bends, with views over the valley from the lookouts. Trucks and caravans use it, so watch for slow vehicles, and fog and rain can reduce visibility. Spicers Gap Road is an alternative, partly unsealed, and can be closed after heavy rain, so check conditions.

Laidley, a town of nearly four thousand, has fuel and cafes, and Kalbar, smaller still, has a good bakery. Fill up before the climb, because the park has no services. The rides in this region connect with Lamington National Park, to the south, where the roads wind through bush to guesthouses and tree-top walks.

Spring and autumn are lovely, with mild days and wildflowers, and summers are hot and stormy. Winters can be cold at altitude, with frost and occasional snow on the highest peaks. Take a thermos, because the picnic tables at the lookouts are made for it.
t.teviot state forest@-28.2,152.5:
The Scenic Rim is the name given to the arc of rugged mountains that curves around the south-east corner of Queensland, along the New South Wales border, and Teviot State Forest sits on its western side. It is dry eucalypt country of ironbark and spotted gum, quite different from the rainforest on the wetter slopes nearby, with open woodland, grassy slopes and rocky creek beds. The area is part of the wider Gondwana Rainforests of Australia, a World Heritage area that preserves the largest subtropical rainforest in the world and the remnants of the ancient forests that once covered the supercontinent Gondwana.

The big names of the region are not far. Mount Chinghee National Park, with its small patches of montane rainforest and views from rocky ridges, lies close to the border, and further south the Border Ranges, with their Antarctic beech trees, hold some of the oldest living plant lineages on earth. Teviot Brook runs through the forest, and the whole area is a good place to see wallabies, kangaroos, lyrebirds and colourful parrots. At dusk, the call of the kookaburra echoes across the valleys. Walkers can reach several peaks, including Mount Barney, a spectacular and demanding climb.

For riders, the lure is the road. The Mount Lindesay Highway, which runs through the area, is one of the favourite motorcycling roads of south-east Queensland, with sweeping bends, rolling hills and views of the cone of Mount Lindesay. The forest tracks are another matter, unsealed and sometimes rutted, so a trail bike is better, and rain makes them slippery. Summer brings heat and thunderstorms, and winter is dry and pleasant, with cold mornings. Watch for wildlife on the road at dawn and dusk, especially kangaroos and wallabies, which can appear suddenly.

Boonah, about thirty kilometres away, has fuel, a bakery and a pub, and Kalbar is a similar small town. The nearest services are not close, so fill the tank and carry water. Be careful of snakes and ticks in the bush, and check the status of the forest tracks with the local authorities before you set off.
t.springbrook national park@-28.2,153.3:
South of the Gold Coast, the land rises suddenly into a plateau of ancient rainforest, waterfalls and cliffs, and this is Springbrook. The plateau is about nine hundred metres high, and it is what remains of the huge Tweed shield volcano, which erupted some twenty-three million years ago and left a vast eroded caldera, with Mount Warning as its central plug. The rim of the caldera forms the Scenic Rim around it, and Springbrook's cliffs and gorges are part of that rim. It is part of the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia, a World Heritage area, and its cool, wet forest is a startling contrast to the beaches and high-rises thirty minutes away.

What you come for is the water and the trees. Purling Brook Falls drops more than a hundred metres into a rainforest gorge, the Natural Bridge is a basalt cave where a creek has bored through the rock, and at night, glow-worms light up the ceiling like a field of stars. On the higher ground, the Antarctic beech, a tree that has survived since the days of Gondwana, grows in mossy, mist-bound groves, some of the trees being thousands of years old. The Best of All Lookout gives views over the volcano's remains and, on a clear day, to the Pacific.

The ride up from Mudgeeraba is excellent: Springbrook Road climbs the escarpment in a series of tight bends and hairpins through eucalypt forest, with a surface that is mostly good but narrow, and occasional wet leaves and gravel. It is popular with riders at weekends, so the best time is a weekday or an early morning. The weather on the plateau is often cooler and wetter than on the coast, with mist and drizzle, so wear a waterproof layer. In summer, afternoon storms are common.

Fuel is not available on the plateau, and the nearest places for it are Mudgeeraba and Reedy Creek, in the Gold Coast hinterland. There is a small cafe or two near the lookouts, and good pies. Take water for the walks, and watch for leeches in the wet season. A visit at dusk to see the glow-worms is worth the effort.
t.mount mistake national park@-27.9,152.4:
Mount Mistake has a name that sounds like an apology. It stands in the Great Dividing Range in south-east Queensland, in rugged country west of Brisbane, and the national park around it protects steep slopes of dry eucalypt forest and a handful of rocky ridgelines. The mountain is not a famous summit, and the park is not set up for casual visitors: this is the kind of bush where the main facilities are the road, the sky and your own sense of direction.

That is what makes it good for a rider who likes the quieter ends of the map. The nearest town is Laidley, about 26 km away and home to some 3,700 people, and the larger centre of Gatton, around 35 km off, has more shops and fuel. Kalbar and Plainland are in the same loose cluster, and this part of the Lockyer Valley is farm country: broad paddocks of lucerne, vegetables and cattle, with the range rising blue behind them. Fill the tank in Laidley or Gatton, since the roads that lead toward the park have nothing along them.

Expect narrow country roads, some of them tight and bumpy, with sections of gravel as you get closer to the range. After heavy rain, creeks can run over the road and the dirt becomes slippery, so check conditions before you set out, especially in the wet season from roughly November to March. Winter and early spring are far kinder, with dry days, clear air and cool mornings. The bush is full of life: wallabies, the occasional koala in the gums, and a noisy chorus of birds at dawn, with kookaburras and rosellas the usual suspects.

Do not underestimate the heat or the distance. In summer the temperature in the valley climbs quickly, and mobile coverage thins out as the road climbs into the hills. Carry water, tell someone where you are headed, and respect any closure signs, which are posted for fire danger and flooding. The Lockyer Valley is also where many Brisbane riders go for a Sunday run, so you may find a few other bikes on the better roads, and a pie and a coffee in a country bakery in Laidley or Gatton is the traditional reward at the end.
t.gibraltar ranger national park@-29.5,152:
Gibraltar Range National Park lies on the high edge of the New South Wales Northern Tablelands, in a part of the country where granite rules. The range is a broad plateau at about a thousand metres, strewn with huge boulders, crags and rounded domes of grey rock, and covered in a mix of heath, eucalypt forest and, in the damp gullies, patches of rainforest. The Dandahra Crags and the Needles are the best-known rock formations, and the walks to them take you through low flowering shrubs that attract honeyeaters in spring.

The park forms part of the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia, a World Heritage group that preserves some of the oldest forest types on the planet, plants whose ancestors were here when Australia was still joined to Antarctica. Nearby Washpool National Park contains stands of ancient tree ferns and giant eucalypts. The climate is cool and often wet, with mist in the mornings, a fine drizzle even in summer, and cold nights. Platypus swim in the creeks, and you may hear lyrebirds calling in the undergrowth. The smell after rain, of wet eucalypt and earth, is a considerable pleasure.

The road through the area is the Gwydir Highway, which crosses the range between Glen Innes on the tableland and Grafton on the coastal plain. The western stretch is a broad, open road, but as it crosses the range it becomes more twisting, with long curves, steep descents and forest on both sides, and the surface is generally fair. Fog, damp patches and logging trucks mean you must pay attention, and wildlife on the road is a hazard at dusk. A mild day in autumn or spring is the best time to be here, and winter can bring frost, ice and even snow in the higher parts.

Services are thin on the range itself, and the data lists no nearby town, so plan around the bigger places. Take fuel in Glen Innes, which has several thousand people and a full set of services, or in Grafton on the coast side, and carry a warm layer, water and some food. Phone reception is patchy in the gullies, and a puncture or breakdown can mean a long wait. Camping areas in the park are basic but well kept, and they are a good way to hear the forest at night.
t.iluka nature reserve@-29.4,153.4:
Iluka is the sort of place that people drive past on the Pacific Highway without noticing, and that is a pity. The town sits at the mouth of the Clarence River on the northern coast of New South Wales, a fishing village of about two thousand people on the opposite bank to Yamba, with a long surf beach on one side and the wide river on the other. A mineral-sands mining company that began here took its name from the place, which is as good a proof as any that this is real working country.

The reserve is what matters. Iluka Nature Reserve is a thin strip of rainforest growing right behind the beach, on the dunes, and it is a rare thing: coastal rainforest that grows in sand, on the very edge of the sea, exposed to salt wind. It is part of the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia, a World Heritage group of reserves that preserve forest descended from the ancient supercontinent. Strangler figs, hoop pines, tuckeroo and cabbage-tree palms crowd the track, and the canopy is loud with birds. Walking in from the headland at the north end, the light turns green and the sound of the surf is muffled almost at once.

For a rider, this is a gentle, flat, coastal start rather than a technical one. The road in follows the river through cane fields and paddocks, with big skies, long straight sections, and ferries or bridges at the river crossings. Traffic is light, apart from school holidays. When you leave, the ride swings inland towards the ranges and the Lamington plateau across the Queensland border, and the road quickly becomes bendy and green as the hills close in. Watch for kangaroos at dawn and dusk and for cattle trucks along the main road.

Iluka has fuel and a couple of cafes, and Yamba, a bigger town of nearly seven thousand across the river, has more of everything. Fresh prawns and fish are the right lunch, and the local fish shops sell them. Winter is dry, mild and the best season; summer is humid and thundery. Wear insect repellent in the forest and don't leave your helmet on the ground unless you want to share it with ants.
t.monchegorsk@67.9,32.9:
Monchegorsk exists because of a rock. Geologists found copper and nickel in the hills of the Kola Peninsula in the 1930s, and a smelter and a town went up in the tundra beside Lake Imandra, well north of the Arctic Circle. The plant, now run by Nornickel, is still the heart of the place, and its smoke over many decades did terrible damage to the surrounding forest. West of town you can see pale, bare slopes where trees once stood, an odd reminder of how industry left its mark on the Arctic.

The landscape around is open and strong. The low, bald ridges of the Monche tundra rise just to the west, Lake Monchegorsk lies at the city's edge, and the huge lake Imandra stretches to the south and east, with the Khibiny Mountains rising on its far shore. In summer the sun does not set for weeks, and the tundra turns green, red and gold with berries and dwarf birch. In winter the polar night closes in for weeks, snow lies deep, and the aurora flickers over the town on clear nights. Reindeer herders and the Sami people have lived here for thousands of years, and some villages keep their traditions.

Riding in the region is sparse and long. The road system is thin, with a few main roads linking the mining towns, and the tarmac can be patched, with frost heaves that appear without warning. Traffic is light apart from lorries from the mines. The riding season is short, from June to early September, and the weather can turn cold and wet at any time. Mosquitoes in July are fierce.

Monchegorsk has about fifty thousand people, so fuel, shops, cafes and hotels are easy, and Olenegorsk, about twenty-eight kilometres away, and the small town of Vysokiy offer some more. Beyond these, services thin out quickly, so fill the tank and carry water. A drive to the viewpoint over the tundra at midnight in June, with the sky glowing orange, is the best reason to be here. Foreign riders should check the current rules for travel before planning.
t.apatity@67.6,33.4:
Apatity takes its name from apatite, the pale green mineral rich in phosphate that was found in the Khibiny Mountains in the late 1920s. The find, led by the geologist Alexander Fersman and his team, started a mining boom that created towns in the tundra, and Apatity, which became a city in 1966, grew as the base for the processing works. It sits on the edge of Lake Imandra, with the dark, flat-topped Khibiny rising to the north, and has the plain, practical look of a Soviet town, with big apartment blocks and long straight streets.

The Khibiny are the real draw. These old mountains, rounded and cut by glaciers, rise to about twelve hundred metres, with deep valleys, boulder fields and lakes in hollows, and they hold one of the richest collections of rare minerals in the world. Kirovsk, twelve kilometres away, is the little mining town at their foot, with a ski resort on the slopes of Mount Aikuaivenchorr and a polar-alpine botanical garden that is the northernmost in Europe. The Sami called the mountains Umptek, and legends of their sacred places remain.

On the road, expect a quiet, open landscape of low birch, tundra and lakes. The main highway between Apatity and Kirovsk is decent, but the side roads and tracks that climb toward the mountains are gravel, rutted and often wet. The season is short, from June to September, and weather can swing from warm sun to sleet within an hour. In late summer, the first frosts turn the tundra red, and in winter the aurora shows over town on clear nights. Midnight sun in June is a bonus, though the mosquitoes can be tough.

Apatity has about sixty thousand people, so fuel, food and repairs are easy to find, and Kirovsk offers more. Before heading into the hills, fill up and carry water. Local food runs to fish, reindeer and cloudberry jam, and a pot of tea in a cafe is welcome after the cold. Foreign riders should check what is currently allowed before planning a trip here.
t.washpool national park@-29.4,152.3:
Washpool is one of those places that people drive past without knowing, which is a shame, because it holds some of the most extensive old-growth rainforest in New South Wales. It lies on the rugged escarpment of the Great Dividing Range between Glen Innes and Grafton, a landscape of granite domes, deep gullies and cool, dripping forest that is part of the Gondwana Rainforests World Heritage Area. The trees include coachwood, a tall, smooth-barked species that forms dense canopy, and ancient stands of Antarctic beech on the higher ground, alongside tree ferns and mosses.

The nearest main road is the Gwydir Highway, which crosses the range between the tablelands and the coast and is one of the more rewarding east-west routes in the region. The road climbs and twists, with long, open sweeps through eucalypt forest and the occasional view over the Clarence valley, and it passes the turn-off to the park. Parts of the highway are fast and open, and parts are tight and shaded, so conditions change quickly, particularly with morning mist or after rain. Heavy trucks use the route, so patience is a virtue.

Within the park, the tracks are largely unsealed, and a few are suited to small bikes only. Coombadjha Creek, which runs through the heart of the forest, has a clear pool for swimming in warm months, and a short walking track follows it through the trees. Platypus and a variety of birds live along the creek, and the call of lyrebirds and whipbirds fills the forest in the early morning. The campground at Coombadjha is a good base for walks.

For supplies, the nearest big towns are Glen Innes, on the tablelands, and Grafton on the coast, and both have fuel, shops and accommodation. The tablelands are also considerably colder than the coast, and winter nights can drop below freezing, so a warm layer is sensible.

Visit in spring, when the wildflowers bloom and the creeks run clear, or in autumn, when the air is crisp and the crowds are thin.
t.baraboo@43.5,-89.7:
Baraboo is a small city in a very old landscape. The ridges that curl around it, the Baraboo Range, are among the most ancient rock formations in the Midwest, made of tough pink quartzite laid down well over a billion years ago and later pushed up into a crescent of bluffs that glaciers then flowed around, not over. The most famous piece of this is Devil's Lake, a deep, clear lake held in a gorge, with sheer purple cliffs above and a state park that is one of the most visited in Wisconsin.

In the town, a different kind of history lives. The Ringling Brothers began their circus in Baraboo in 1884, and the winter quarters of the show stood here for decades. Circus World, a museum on the old grounds beside the Baraboo River, preserves wagons, posters and the sights and smells of the big top, and the Al Ringling Theatre, a plush opera house from 1915, still stands downtown. Southeast of town, the little shack where Aldo Leopold wrote part of A Sand County Almanac, the landmark book of the conservation movement, stands in a quiet field and is open to visitors.

The riding is the sort the Midwest does quietly well. Roads through the range wind over rises and down into valleys, with farmland and forest, and the lanes toward the Wisconsin River and the Kickapoo country have easy curves and a sense of space. Wisconsin Highway 33 and 23 run west, while county roads loop through hills where hawks and turkey vultures turn in the thermals. The surface is generally good, though some county roads have frost heaves, and the Amish buggies seen in the western hills deserve caution.

Baraboo has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, and Lake Delton and Wisconsin Dells nearby supply plenty of hotels and attractions, though those places are crowded in summer. The International Crane Foundation, just north, houses all fifteen species of crane in the world. The best time is early October, with color and cool air, but June is lovely too. Midsummer weekends bring heavy traffic around the Dells, so start early. Winter is cold, with snow and ice, and thunderstorms in summer can be violent, with brief hail.
t.traverse city@44.8,-85.6:
Cherries explain Traverse City. The sandy soil and the moderating influence of Grand Traverse Bay, which keeps late frosts at bay, make this corner of Michigan the biggest tart-cherry producer in the country, and the town holds a National Cherry Festival each July with parades, pies and fireworks. In May the orchards on the hills blossom white, and by mid-summer the roadside stands are heaped with red fruit. More recently the same climate has produced a flourishing wine country, with vineyards on the Leelanau and Old Mission peninsulas.

The bay is the heart of the place. Two long fingers of land, the Leelanau and Old Mission peninsulas, enclose its two arms, and the water is a startling blue-green in clear weather. Downtown Traverse City runs along the shore, with a boardwalk, a harbor, and a main street of restaurants, bookshops and breweries. It is a lively place, in some ways too popular in July, when the beaches and sidewalks fill up, but the setting more than carries it.

For riders, the loop that matters is M-22, the highway that circles the Leelanau Peninsula. It runs along the shoreline through small villages, orchards and dunes, with water views at nearly every turn, and the surface is generally good. Leland, a little harbor town, has Fishtown, a cluster of weathered fishing shanties from the nineteenth century that remain in use, and farther south Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore, named for an Ojibwe legend of a mother bear waiting for her cubs, has towering sand bluffs above Lake Michigan. In 2011 viewers of a morning television show voted it the most beautiful place in America.

Traverse City has every service: fuel, supermarkets, hotels and plenty of food. Kingsley, to the south, is a small town if you head that way. The best time is September, when the water is still warm, the crowds are lighter and the colors are beginning to turn, though June is also pleasant. Midsummer weekends bring slow traffic and full parking lots. Winter brings lake-effect snow, which closes many of the scenic roads, so most visitors come between May and October. Fog off the bay can slow the morning start.
t.brisbane@-27.5,153.0:
Brisbane winds along its river like a long, lazy snake, with the city centre in one loop and suburbs spreading over low hills on every side. It began in 1825 as a penal settlement, chosen for its position on the Brisbane River, and grew slowly into the capital of Queensland. A humid subtropical climate means jacaranda trees blaze purple in October and November, thunderstorms roll in on summer afternoons, and the winters are mild and sunny, ideal for riding. The Story Bridge, the riverside parks at South Bank and the ferries that glide up and down the water give the city a relaxed charm.

The city has its own riding scene, with weekend crowds heading to the cafes at Mount Glorious and the Gold Coast hinterland. To the north, the Blackall Range rises abruptly from the coastal plain, with a scenic road running along its crest through Montville and Maleny, past rainforest, art shops and tea houses, with views over the Glass House Mountains, a cluster of volcanic plugs that stand up from the plain like giant tooth stumps. To the south and west, the border ranges around Mount Barney and the Lions Road wind through steep forest on the line between Queensland and New South Wales, with sections that have been unsealed in the past, so check conditions before you go.

Brisbane's own traffic is heavy at peak times, and the motorways have electronic tolls, which are charged by number plate, so check how to pay for them. Speed cameras are common, and Queensland police are firm on limits and on helmets. In spring, magpies swoop on riders near nests, so keep your visor down and ride on if one dives. Fuel stations are everywhere in the city and on the main roads, but they become rare in the hills, so keep an eye on your tank.

The best months for riding are April to October, when the humidity drops and the air is clear. Summer storms can be fierce, with hail and flash flooding, so watch the sky.
t.somerset dam@-27.1,152.5:
Somerset Dam holds back the Stanley River in the hills north-west of Brisbane, and its wide, quiet lake is one of the best-kept secrets of the Brisbane Valley. The dam was begun in the 1930s and finished in the 1950s, partly to supply water and partly to control flooding, and it forms Lake Somerset, a long arm of blue water winding among forested hills. Brisbane suffered badly in the great flood of 1974, and a bigger dam, Wivenhoe, was built downstream afterward to protect the city.

The area is popular with locals for fishing, boating and picnicking, and the lake has a number of recreation areas where families gather. Swimming is allowed in designated areas, but should be approached with sense, since dams have sudden drop-offs, submerged timber and cold water below the surface. Check signs before getting in, and do not jump from heights. Bass and golden perch are stocked in the lake, and the fishing is well regarded.

The riding on the way is good. The roads from Brisbane, through Samford and up Mount Glorious, are winding and shady, with views across the rainforest, and the surface is generally good. The Mount Glorious road is one of the best motorcycle roads near the city, a tight and twisty ride through subtropical forest, so it is popular and often busy with riders at weekends. Police patrols are frequent. Further on, the road passes through Kilcoy and across the farmland of the Brisbane Valley, with rolling pastures and gum trees. Lyrebirds and brush turkeys scratch in the forest, and in the early morning, the air smells of eucalyptus and damp earth.

Weather in south-east Queensland is warm to hot, with summer afternoon storms that can be fierce, with heavy rain and lightning. Check the sky before setting off, and avoid exposed spots during storms. Winter is mild and dry, and the best time for riding. Spring brings wildflowers.

Services around the dam are limited. There is a small township, and a few cafes may be open at weekends, but fuel is a matter of planning. Esk, Kilcoy and Toogoolawah all have stations within twenty kilometres, and are the usual places to fill up. Bring water, sunscreen and insect repellent, and be prepared for the heat.
t.esk@-27.2,152.4:
Esk is a small country town in the Brisbane Valley, about eighty kilometres north-west of Brisbane, and a handy place to stop on a day in the hills. It sits on the Brisbane Valley Highway, with fertile farmland all around, growing lucerne, grain and vegetables, and grazing cattle. The town has a classic main street, with a pub, a bakery, a few shops, and a war memorial, and the pace is pleasantly slow. The district was settled in the 1840s by pastoralists, and the town grew with the railway, which brought the produce of the valley to the city.

The railway is gone, but the old line has been converted to the Brisbane Valley Rail Trail, a long cycle and walking path through the countryside. The valley, with its soft hills and the broad green flats beside the Brisbane River, makes a gentle contrast with the rainforest roads of Mount Glorious. Nearby, Lake Wivenhoe, the large reservoir built after the 1974 floods, holds much of Brisbane's water and acts as a flood buffer. Its shores have parks and walks, and the area is popular for fishing and kayaking.

The riding around Esk is easy and enjoyable. Roads such as the Esk-Hampton road and the road to Toogoolawah run through rolling pasture, with long views and light traffic. Corners are mostly open and flowing, and the surfaces are good, though cattle grids and the occasional pothole call for a little care. Kangaroos and wallabies feed along the verges at dawn and dusk, and cattle sometimes cross the road. In summer, heat can be intense, and storms build quickly in the afternoon.

For a rider, the town is a service stop with a rural flavour. Fuel is available in the main street, and there are places for a meal or coffee, with a bakery that is a traditional stop for pies. Parking is easy, and the locals are friendly to travellers. Gatton, thirty-eight kilometres to the south, is a larger town with more choice.

Winter and early spring are the nicest times, with cool mornings and clear skies. On a Sunday, the town fills with riders on their way to and from the lakes and hills.
t.sturgeon bay@44.8,-87.4:
Door County is the thumb of Wisconsin, a limestone peninsula that sticks into Lake Michigan like a hitchhiker's hand, and Sturgeon Bay is the town where you come in. It is the only real city on the peninsula, with about nine thousand people, a shipyard, a downtown that climbs a hill from the water, and a ship canal that makes the northern half of Door County, in effect, an island. The canal was cut in 1881 to connect Green Bay with Lake Michigan, saving ships the long, dangerous trip around the tip, and it is crossed by a steel bridge that lifts to let freighters through. If you are held up there, watch for the long, low ships sliding past at head height.

The shipyards have built vessels here for more than a century, from wooden schooners to Great Lakes freighters and, in more recent years, large naval ships. That industrial skyline is part of the town's character, set beside the restaurants and galleries that serve visitors. The surrounding orchards are cherry and apple, and Door County is famous for its cherries, in pies and in dried form. You should also try a fish boil, a local ritual in which whitefish and potatoes are cooked in a kettle over a wood fire, with a dramatic boil-over of salty froth. It is as much theatre as dinner.

Sturgeon Bay is practical for a rider. Fuel is easy, groceries and coffee are plentiful, and accommodation is spread across town. From here, state highways run north along either shore, through pretty towns and past farm stands. The riding is gentle rather than technical: gentle bends, long views to the water, and a lot of cars in summer and autumn. Weekends in July and October, when the leaves turn, are slow and crowded, so aim for a weekday morning. Winds off the lake can be strong, and fog sometimes rolls in during spring.

The peninsula's limestone bedrock is part of the Niagara Escarpment, the same ridge that makes the falls, and it shows in the white cliffs on the Green Bay side and the cobbled beaches on the lake side. Lighthouses are scattered along the shore.

Fill the tank, eat well, and then turn north. The best of the peninsula is still ahead of you.
t.rabocheostrovsk@65.0,34.8:
Rabocheostrovsk is a small port on the White Sea, and for most travellers it is simply the place the Solovetsky ferry leaves from. It lies on the coast a few kilometres from Kem, the larger town to which it belongs historically, at the point where the railway and the highway from the south meet the open water. The name means Workers' Island, a Soviet rebranding from the 1930s, and the place has the functional look of a harbour: cranes, sheds, a railway siding, and a long jetty reaching into the shallow, cold sea.

The significance is the islands beyond. Solovki, the Solovetsky archipelago, lies about sixty kilometres offshore, and it carries the weight of Russian history: a great monastery founded in the fifteenth century by the monks Savvaty, Zosima and German, which became one of the most powerful in the country, then a prison and later the first camp of the Soviet Gulag. The White Sea can be flat as glass on a June morning and rough by afternoon.

Kem, ten kilometres away, is worth a visit for its wooden Assumption Cathedral, built in the early eighteenth century, a tall, tent-roofed building painted white and green, which is one of the great surviving wooden churches of the north. Kem was also a transit point for prisoners headed for Solovki in the 1920s and 30s, and the town carries that history quietly. The local sea food is simple and good, and you may find smoked fish and fresh bread in small shops.

The road here is the long Kola highway, a good modern surface with long straights, rolling forest and occasional wet patches, and the final approach to the port is short. Traffic includes long-distance trucks, so ride with care, especially in rain. Summer brings midnight sun and mosquitoes, while autumn brings low cloud and cold wind off the sea. Winter is dark and brutal, and ferries do not run.

Fuel is at Kem, which has several stations, and it is best to fill up there before you reach the port. The port village itself is small, with a few shops and a cafe or two, and it is simplest to arrive with a plan. Walk to the end of the jetty and look out at the sea. It is cold, wide, and very northern.
t.kalevala@65.2,31.2:
Kalevala is the town that renamed itself after a poem. It used to be Uhtua, a Finnish-speaking Karelian village on the shore of Lake Ukhta, in the borderland where Finns and Russians had mingled for centuries, and in 1963 it took the name of the national epic, in honour of what had been collected here. The story goes that in the 1830s, the Finnish doctor Elias Lönnrot walked through the villages of Russian Karelia, listening to the old rune singers who recited the ancient songs, and from what he gathered, he assembled the Kalevala, the epic of Väinämöinen, Ilmarinen and the magic Sampo. It was published in 1835 and enlarged in 1849, and it became the foundation of Finnish national identity, and later inspired Sibelius and Tolkien.

The town today has about five thousand people, scattered around a lake in dense forest, with wooden houses, a few Soviet blocks, and a small museum devoted to the epic. It is close to the Finnish border, and the Finnish influence is still visible in the place names and the landscape. The air smells of resin and wet moss, and the lakes are dark and clear.

The ride through here, from Kostomuksha, follows quiet forest roads through some of the most remote country in European Russia. The taiga is spruce and pine, with bogs, ridges and countless lakes, and in the long summer light it can feel endless. Road quality varies, so be ready for patches, frost heave and the occasional gravel stretch, and keep your speed down, because elk, reindeer and even bears can cross the road. Mosquitoes are bad from June to August. The best months are late May, June, and September, when the forest turns gold.

Fuel and food are available in town, which has a petrol station and shops, but beyond it supplies are thin, so fill up here. There is little traffic, so a breakdown can mean a long wait, and it is wise to carry water, a repair kit and some food. The border zone is nearby, and you should carry your documents, and check whether permits are needed for areas close to the frontier.

Walk to the lake, listen to the loons, and think of a doctor with a notebook, a century and a half ago.
t.pechenga@69.5,31.2:
Pechenga is a name with several lives. Before 1920 it was a remote monastery on the Arctic coast, founded in 1533 by Saint Tryphon, a monk who walked north to convert the Sami and built a chapel in the wilderness. After the Russian Revolution, the area passed to Finland, which called it Petsamo and gave the country its only outlet on the Arctic Ocean, until the Second World War, when the Soviet Union took it back in 1944. The monastery had been bombed, and was rebuilt after 1991, and today a handful of monks live there again, in a quiet valley of birch and spruce near the river.

The settlement around it is small, with fewer than three thousand people, and the nearest sizeable town is Zapolyarny, about nineteen kilometres off, with Nikel farther on. These are mining towns, built around the huge deposits of nickel and copper in the surrounding hills, and the smelters have left a hard mark on the land, with burnt hills and bare ground around them. The contrast between the industrial lunar landscape and the green river valleys is striking. Norway lies just across the border, and the country is a militarised frontier zone, so carry your passport and check whether permits are required for areas near the border.

The ride from Murmansk is long and fairly empty. Through tundra and low forest, the road runs west past lakes and low hills, with a decent surface in places and frost damage in others, and trucks carrying ore. The weather is changeable, with wind, fog and sleet in any month. In summer, midnight sun lasts for weeks, and the light is soft and golden in the evenings. Autumn colours are splendid in September, and winter is dark and brutally cold.

Fuel is no problem in Zapolyarny and Nikel, which have petrol stations and shops, but supplies thin out toward the coast, so fill up before you go further. Pechenga itself has a few shops, and the monastery is open to visitors who dress modestly. If you want to eat, local cafés serve simple hot meals.

The area has been disputed, divided and fought over, and it carries traces of war: ruined bunkers, old Finnish buildings, and cemeteries. A few moments by the river, hearing the bells of the monastery, give you a clear sense of how strange this corner of the world is.
t.sredny peninsula@69.6,32.4:
The peninsula and its neighbour Rybachy were the front line of the northern war. In 1941, German mountain troops attacked from Norway, aiming for Murmansk, and were stopped here on the Zapadnaya Litsa river after months of fighting. The line held until 1944, and the hills are littered with concrete bunkers, rusted barbed wire, and the foundations of gun positions. Today the area is a closed border zone, and the Northern Fleet's submarine bases lie close by, so access normally requires a permit, which should be arranged well ahead, and the rules can change.

The landscape is spare and beautiful. The ground is a mix of bare granite, bog and low scrub, with dwarf birch and juniper in sheltered hollows, crowberry and cloudberry across the flats, and lakes in every dip. The sea is cold and green. In summer, the light never really goes, and the colours are soft and bright. In autumn, the tundra turns red and orange, and the first snow comes in September or October. Reindeer and sea eagles are not uncommon, and you may see seals along the shore.

Expect broken slabs, potholes, mud and wind, and be ready for fog that cuts visibility to a few metres. A dual-sport bike, a puncture kit, and a plan for the weather are the minimum. The wind can blow so hard that it is hard to stand, and summer temperatures hover around ten degrees. Mosquitoes in July are vicious on the sheltered side of the hills.

Fuel is the main practical constraint. There are no services on the peninsula, and no mobile coverage in places, so bring food, water, a repair kit and warm clothes.

The tundra is quiet, the war is long over, and the sea is endless. Come for the light.
t.rybachy peninsula@69.9,32.9:
Rybachy, the Fisherman's Peninsula, is the northernmost tip of mainland Russia's western Arctic coast, a block of tundra and sea cliff jutting into the Barents Sea. The name comes from the fishing communities that the Pomors established here in the Middle Ages, in summer camps on the shore, and the peninsula was an important base for cod and halibut fishing for centuries. Until 1940, much of it belonged to Finland, as part of the Petsamo region, and the Soviet Union held it afterwards. During the Second World War, it was the line where the German advance stopped, and the coast bristled with Soviet guns.

The landscape is bare and dramatic. A line of cliffs, hundreds of feet high at Cape Nemetsky, plunges into the sea, with seabird colonies of kittiwakes, guillemots and puffins nesting on the ledges in summer. Behind the coast, the tundra stretches in low rolling folds, with boulders left by glaciers, shallow lakes, and drifts of cloudberry. The geology, a mix of old sandstone and shale, gives the shore a layered look. Sea eagles patrol the cliffs, and the sea beyond is dark blue. On a clear day, with the sun low, the view across the water goes on forever.

Reaching it is a project. The peninsula is in the border zone, and you need a permit from the border authorities to enter, so apply well ahead and have your documents ready. Expect mud, potholes, and sudden fog, and keep your speed down. Wind is a constant companion, and the weather can change in minutes. Summer, late June to August, is the only practical season, with long daylight, and temperatures rarely above fifteen degrees.

Fuel, food and repairs must come from Murmansk or the larger settlements on the mainland, and you should carry spare fuel and a basic repair kit. Mobile coverage is patchy, and help is far away, so travel with a companion if you can and tell someone your plan.

The lighthouse and the old batteries are worth a look, and on a calm evening the sea is a pale gold. It feels like the edge of the world, and in many ways it is.
t.border ranges national park@-28.3,152.9:
Twenty three million years ago a huge shield volcano stood over what is now the border between New South Wales and Queensland, and the Border Ranges are the remains of its northern and western rim. The volcano has long since eroded, leaving a vast caldera with the steep central plug of Wollumbin, also known as Mount Warning, rising in the middle, and a ring of cliffs and ridges around it covered in dense subtropical rainforest. The Border Ranges National Park protects a large part of that rim, and it is part of the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia, a World Heritage Site that preserves forests whose ancestry goes back to the time when Australia was part of the supercontinent Gondwana.

The forests are full of ancient trees, including Antarctic beeches, some of them thousands of years old, as well as tree ferns, strangler figs, palms and epiphytes. The wildlife includes Albert's lyrebird, a shy bird with a remarkable gift for mimicry, pademelons, possums, frogs and a great variety of birds. The views from the escarpment edge, at lookouts such as the Pinnacle, over the caldera to Wollumbin and the coast, are among the finest in eastern Australia.

The Tweed Range Scenic Drive runs through the park along the rim, a gravel road of about sixty kilometres, with steep, narrow sections, tight bends and loose surfaces. It is suitable for bikes ridden with care, but it can become slippery after rain, and it may be closed after storms. For sealed-road riders, the area has something even better: the Lions Road, running from near Kyogle across the range at Richmond Gap to Rathdowney in Queensland, is one of the most popular motorcycle roads in the region, with tight bends through rainforest and farmland, and views over the valleys.

Kyogle, about thirty kilometres away, is a small country town with fuel, shops and cafes, and Kooralbyn is on the Queensland side. There are no services in the park itself, so carry water and food, and fill up before you go. Watch out for wildlife on the roads, especially at dawn and dusk, when wallabies and kangaroos are most active. The weather is subtropical, with hot, wet summers and mild, dry winters, the best time to ride.
t.spicers gap state forest@-28.1,152.4:
Allan Cunningham, the botanist and explorer, found a way through the Main Range in 1827, and the gap that bears his name now carries the busy highway from Brisbane to the Darling Downs. A few kilometres to the south, Spicers Gap was the route that early drays and coaches used instead, because it offered an easier climb up the escarpment. The old road, built in the mid nineteenth century with stone retaining walls and drains that can still be seen, is now part of the Main Range National Park and the neighbouring state forest, and it is a fascinating relic of the pioneer days, with a historic cemetery and the remains of an old camping ground for teamsters.

The Main Range is the western rim of the Scenic Rim, a chain of mountains running along the border of Queensland and New South Wales, part of the Gondwana Rainforests World Heritage area. The forests here are a mix of eucalyptus woodland and rainforest, with tall trees, vines, ferns and moss-covered rocks, and the wildlife includes koalas, wallabies, lyrebirds and many birds. The views from lookouts along the range, over the Fassifern Valley to the east and the Darling Downs to the west, are superb.

The Spicers Gap road is gravel, narrow and steep in places, with loose surfaces and ruts, and it is best tackled on a bike suited to dirt roads, in dry weather. The highway through Cunningham's Gap, on the other hand, is sealed and busy, with heavy trucks, so it is better to ride it outside peak times. The roads around Boonah and Kalbar, in the farmland below the range, are quiet and scenic, with gentle bends, rolling hills and views of the mountains. Lake Moogerah, a reservoir surrounded by peaks, is a popular spot for picnics and water sports.

Boonah, about twenty eight kilometres away, is a small country town with fuel, shops and cafes, and Kalbar is a historic village settled by German immigrants. There are no services in the forest, so carry water and food. The weather is subtropical, with hot summers and occasional heavy storms, and mild, dry winters, when the riding is at its best. Watch out for wildlife on the roads, especially at dawn and dusk, and be aware of bushfire danger in hot, dry conditions.
t.cronan creek state forest@-28.3,152.7:
Cronan Creek runs off the slopes of Mount Barney, one of the great peaks of the Scenic Rim, the arc of mountains along the Queensland and New South Wales border southwest of Brisbane. Mount Barney rises to over thirteen hundred metres, a rugged mass of volcanic rock covered in eucalyptus forest, with rainforest in the gullies and heathland near the summit, and it is the most challenging climb in southeast Queensland. The creek valley below is quiet and lovely, with clear water running over rocks, tall gums and grassy flats where wallabies graze at dusk.

The area is part of the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia, a World Heritage listing that covers dozens of protected areas along the Great Dividing Range in Queensland and New South Wales. The rainforests here are remnants of the forests that covered the ancient supercontinent of Gondwana, with plants whose ancestors go back to the age of dinosaurs. Birds are everywhere: kookaburras laughing in the morning, black cockatoos, whipbirds cracking their calls through the forest, and, if you are lucky, the shy Albert's lyrebird.

The roads around here are excellent for riding. The Boonah to Rathdowney road crosses the farmland and foothills with good curves and views of the mountains, and the Mount Lindesay Highway runs south from Rathdowney across the border into New South Wales, winding through forest and over the range. Smaller roads, some unsealed, lead to the trailheads around Mount Barney and Cronan Creek. Watch for kangaroos and wallabies, especially at dawn and dusk, and for cattle on unfenced roads. Gravel roads can be corrugated and slippery after rain.

There are no services at the creek itself. Rathdowney, a small country town, has fuel, a general store and a pub; Boonah, about thirty-five kilometres to the northwest, and Beaudesert are larger towns with more choice. Kooralbyn is a resort community with a few facilities. Summer brings heat, humidity and storms, sometimes with flooding that closes roads; winter is cool and dry, ideal for riding and walking. Carry water and sun protection, and be aware of snakes in warmer months. The view of Mount Barney at sunset from the farmland, the mountain glowing red above the green paddocks, is a classic of the region.
t.goomburra state forest@-28.0,152.4:
Goomburra is the northern gateway to Main Range National Park, a section of the Great Dividing Range west of Brisbane where the mountains rise steeply from the Darling Downs and the Fassifern valley. Like its neighbours on the range it belongs to the Gondwana Rainforests, and it is a place of mountain forest, rainforest gullies and dramatic lookouts. Dalrymple Creek flows through the valley, lined with tall eucalypts and rainforest, and the camping area beside it is a favourite of families and walkers.

The road in, Inverramsay Road, leaves the Cunningham Highway near Allora and runs east through farmland into the hills, before climbing on a narrow, winding and partly unsealed road through the forest to the lookouts at Mount Castle and Sylvesters, from where you look down across the escarpment to the Fassifern valley and the distant ranges of the Scenic Rim. The final stretch is steep and narrow, and in wet weather it can be slippery and muddy; check conditions before you go.

Nearby, Cunningham's Gap is the pass through which the Cunningham Highway crosses the range, named after the explorer Allan Cunningham, who found it in 1827 and opened the way for settlers to the Darling Downs. The highway climbs steeply with tight curves through rainforest, and it is popular with riders, though heavy trucks use it too, and accidents are common. Spicers Gap, a little further south, has an old unsealed road used by bullock teams, now a scenic drive through the forest.

The wildlife here is rich: wallabies, possums, many species of birds including satin bowerbirds and the rare eastern bristlebird, and at night, gliders in the trees. Watch for animals on the roads, especially at dawn and dusk. There are no services at Goomburra itself. Allora, about thirty-seven kilometres away, is a small town with fuel and basic shops, and Warwick, further south, is a larger regional town with everything. Kalbar and Boonah, on the eastern side of the range, are also within reach. Summer brings heat and storms; winter nights can be frosty on the Downs, with clear, crisp days that are perfect for riding.
t.nightcap national park@-28.5,153.3:
Nightcap National Park covers a high, wet plateau and escarpment north of Lismore in New South Wales, the remains of the rim of an ancient volcano centred on Wollumbin, Mount Warning, whose eroded caldera forms one of the largest in the world. The plateau receives some of the highest rainfall in the state, and it is covered in subtropical rainforest, tall eucalypt forest and dramatic waterfalls, including Minyon Falls, which drops about a hundred metres over a cliff of volcanic rock. Nightcap is one of the Gondwana Rainforests reserves, and in 2000 it made headlines when scientists found a previously unknown tree, the Nightcap oak, surviving in only a few small populations here.

The forests here have a special place in Australian environmental history. In 1979, at Terania Creek, protesters blocked loggers from entering the rainforest, in one of the first direct-action environmental campaigns in Australia. The protests led to the protection of the forests and helped inspire the national movement to save rainforests. Protestors Falls, at the end of a short walk in the Terania Creek valley, is named after them.

Nimbin, a few kilometres away, is Australia's best-known alternative town. In 1973 it hosted the Aquarius Festival, which brought thousands of young people seeking a different way of life, and many stayed. Its main street, with psychedelic murals, hemp shops and cafes, is colourful, a bit faded and very much its own place. The surrounding hills are dotted with communes and small farms.

The roads around Nightcap are narrow, winding and often wet, climbing through rainforest and farmland with steep grades, tight bends and occasional unsealed sections, like the road up to Mount Nardi or the Whian Whian forest drive. They are great fun on a dry day but treacherous when wet, with mud, moss and fallen leaves. Watch for wildlife, including pademelons, and for logging trucks and locals who know the roads well. Nimbin has basic shops and cafes; for fuel and a full choice of services, Lismore, Mullumbimby and the coastal towns such as Ocean Shores are better bets. Summer is hot, humid and wet, with storms and flash floods; winter is mild and drier.
t.telemon environmental park@-28.2,152.9:
The country south of Beaudesert, in Queensland's Scenic Rim, is a soft landscape of cattle paddocks, gum-lined creeks and wooded hills that rise steadily towards the volcanic ranges along the New South Wales border. Telemon Environmental Park is one of the small protected patches in these hills, near the resort village of Kooralbyn, a reminder of the open eucalypt forest that once covered the whole area.

This is a great part of south-east Queensland for riding. The Mount Lindesay Highway runs south from Beaudesert past Rathdowney and on towards the border at Mount Lindesay, a road with long sweepers, rolling crests and big views towards the ramparts of Mount Barney and the McPherson Range. Smaller roads branch off it, like the route through Kooralbyn and back towards Boonah, with tighter corners, narrow bridges and fewer cars. Surfaces are generally sealed but can be patchy, with rough edges, potholes and loose gravel on some back roads. Keep watch for kangaroos and wallabies at dawn and dusk, and for cattle wandering onto unfenced stretches. Remember to drive on the left.

The Scenic Rim takes its name from the ring of mountains formed by the remains of ancient volcanoes, including the massive Tweed Volcano further east. Mount Barney, with its craggy granite summits, is one of the most rugged peaks in the region, and Lamington and Main Range National Parks protect large areas of rainforest that are part of the Gondwana Rainforests World Heritage site. Down in the valleys, the Logan and Albert rivers wind through farmland that has been grazed since the nineteenth century.

In the woodlands you may see koalas in the gums, kookaburras laughing from fence posts and flocks of cockatoos screeching overhead. Spring brings wattle blossom and clear, cool mornings, while summer can be hot and stormy, with dramatic afternoon thunderheads building over the ranges.

Beaudesert, about nineteen kilometres away, is the main service town for the area, with fuel, cafés, supermarkets and a pub or two. Kooralbyn has limited services, so do not count on fuel there. Rathdowney, further south, has a small general store and pub that are popular stops with riders, especially on weekends. Carry water on hot days, as shade can be scarce in the paddock country.
t.numinbah nature reserve@-28.2,153.3:
On the New South Wales side of the border range above the Gold Coast hinterland, the land rises into steep, forested ridges that are the eroded rim of the ancient Tweed Volcano. Numinbah Nature Reserve protects a slice of this country, a jumble of rainforest gullies, eucalypt slopes and rocky outcrops, looking south across the great green bowl of the Tweed valley towards the sharp peak of Wollumbin, also known as Mount Warning.

For riders, this area is best known for the road that crosses it. The Nerang–Murwillumbah Road runs from the Gold Coast up the Numinbah Valley, past the Natural Bridge, where a creek pours through the roof of a cave, and over the range into New South Wales before dropping towards Murwillumbah. It is a classic local ride: tight bends through rainforest, sections where the road clings to the hillside, and stunning views over the caldera. Surfaces can be bumpy and patched, and the road is often wet under the canopy, so caution is wise. On weekends it fills with riders, so expect company, and police presence is not unusual.

The Tweed Volcano was active around twenty-three million years ago, and erosion has since carved out the caldera, leaving Wollumbin as the remnant of its central plug. The surrounding rainforests are part of the Gondwana Rainforests World Heritage site, holding plant lineages that go back to the days when Australia was joined to Antarctica. Wollumbin is a sacred site for the local Aboriginal people, and the traditional custodians ask visitors to respect it.

The forest is full of life: brush turkeys scratching in the leaf litter, lyrebirds calling from the undergrowth, pademelons at the edge of clearings at dusk, and glow-worms in sheltered gullies at night. After rain, the waterfalls come alive and the air smells of damp earth and leaves.

Murwillumbah, about fourteen kilometres away, is the nearest town with full services, including fuel, cafés and accommodation, and it has an excellent regional art gallery. On the Queensland side, Nerang and the Gold Coast suburbs have everything you need. Carry water and a rain jacket, since the weather can change quickly in the mountains, and be prepared for slow traffic on the narrowest sections.
t.gilbert state forest@-28.1,152.4:
West of Brisbane, the Great Dividing Range rises as a dark wall above the plains, and Gilbert State Forest sits on its western slopes, where the rainforest of the escarpment gives way to drier eucalypt woodland and the farmland of the Darling Downs. To the east lies Main Range National Park, with its high peaks and steep cliffs; to the west, the land opens out towards Warwick and the wide grain fields beyond.

Getting here is a pleasure in itself. The Cunningham Highway climbs over the range at Cunningham's Gap, a well-graded road with sweeping bends and a short, steep section through rainforest at the top, before descending onto the Downs. It is a busy route with trucks and caravans, so the smaller roads around Goomburra, Emu Vale and the foothills are more appealing. These lanes wander through farmland and forest, with some gravel stretches and sharp corners. The weather can be very different on each side of the range: misty and wet on the eastern scarp, sunny and dry on the Downs. Winter mornings can be frosty on the high ground, and kangaroos are a constant hazard around dawn and dusk.

Cunningham's Gap is named after Allan Cunningham, the botanist and explorer who found the pass in 1827, opening up the rich pastures of the Darling Downs to European settlement. Warwick, the main town nearby, grew as a pastoral centre and is known for its handsome sandstone buildings and its long-running rodeo. The traditional owners of this land include the Githabul and other Aboriginal groups, whose connections to the range go back thousands of years.

The forests of the range are part of the Gondwana Rainforests World Heritage site, with ancient plants and animals such as the Albert's lyrebird. In the drier woodlands you might spot wallabies, echidnas and a variety of parrots. The views from the escarpment lookouts stretch across the Fassifern Valley to the coastal ranges on a clear day.

There are no services in the state forest itself. Warwick, about thirty-five kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, with fuel, food and accommodation. Boonah and Kalbar on the eastern side are smaller but have fuel and cafés. Carry water and plan your fuel stops carefully, especially if you intend to explore the gravel roads.
t.mount nothofagus flora reserve@-28.3,152:
