Nothofagus is the botanical name of the southern beech, and the name of this reserve gives away its treasure: stands of Antarctic beech growing high on the McPherson Range along the Queensland–New South Wales border. These gnarled, moss-covered trees, some of them centuries old and sprouting from root systems far older still, are living relics of the forests that covered Gondwana before Australia drifted away from Antarctica.

The reserve sits in rugged country west of Mount Lindesay, right up against the state border, where volcanic peaks and long ridges rise above the upper Clarence and Condamine valleys. It is a remote corner, with few roads and fewer people. Access is mainly via the Mount Lindesay Highway, which crosses the range between Rathdowney and Woodenbong, offering a mix of open sweepers, tight bends and spectacular views of the border peaks. Beyond the highway, the roads are often unsealed, steep and narrow, and some forest tracks become impassable after heavy rain. The weather on the range can be cool and misty even in summer, and winter brings cold nights and occasional frost.

This country has a long human history. The Githabul people are the traditional custodians of much of this land, and Mount Lindesay and other peaks hold deep significance for them. European settlers came for timber and grazing in the nineteenth century, and the remains of old logging tracks still crisscross the ranges. Today, much of the forest is protected as part of the Gondwana Rainforests World Heritage site.

Walking among the Antarctic beech feels like stepping into another time. The trunks are thick with moss and ferns, the air is cool and damp, and the light filters through the canopy in soft green tones. You might hear the calls of the Albert's lyrebird, see pademelons in the undergrowth, or spot the bright colours of the regent bowerbird. After rain, the forest drips and steams, and the smell of wet earth is intoxicating.

There are no services in the reserve. The nearest towns are Kooralbyn and Boonah, both over thirty kilometres away, and Woodenbong on the New South Wales side is a small village with limited supplies. Carry plenty of fuel, water and food, and let someone know your plans before venturing onto the forest tracks.
t.wilsons peak flora reserve@-28.2,152.5:
The Border Ranges are where Queensland leans against New South Wales, and Wilsons Peak, a rocky summit on the line between the two states, is part of that tumbled wall. The flora reserve around it protects a patch of high, cool forest on the old volcanic ranges, and it is one of those places that the wider world mostly forgets. The land here was shaped by the huge Tweed volcano, which erupted for millions of years, leaving behind a circle of mountains and deep valleys.

Forests on the higher slopes are some of Australia's oldest. Antarctic beech grows in the cool, damp cloud zone, with ferns, orchids and mosses around the trunks. Lower down there are subtropical rainforest and eucalypt forest, filled with the sounds of bellbirds, lyrebirds and rustling wallabies. These forests form part of the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia, a UNESCO listing. The scent after rain, wet bark, leaf litter and cold stone, is unforgettable.

The nearest town is Boonah, over thirty kilometres away, with Kalbar and Kooralbyn further out. These are small country towns, and Boonah is where you should buy fuel, food and anything else you need. Between there and the reserve you are in remote territory, so carry water, a basic repair kit and extra layers, since weather at altitude turns quickly from sunshine to cloud and rain.

The roads leading to the reserve include gravel forestry tracks that suit a trail bike or an adventure machine, though they become slick and rutted after rain, and some are closed in wet weather. The sealed roads in the Scenic Rim, which curve around the valleys below the ranges, are a delight, with long, flowing bends and green paddocks. Spring is superb, with wildflowers and mild days, while winter nights get cold. Check with the Queensland and New South Wales park agencies about closures before you go.
t.turtle rock environmental park@-28.2,153:
The Gold Coast hinterland is the green wall behind the beaches and high-rises of southern Queensland, and it is a steep, wet, forested country of ridges, gorges and waterfalls that climbs toward the New South Wales border. The nearby ranges belong to the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia, a UNESCO site said to protect the largest area of subtropical rainforest in the world.

The rock itself tells a story. About twenty-three million years ago a huge volcano, the Tweed volcano, rose here, and its eroded remains form a giant ring of mountains around a central plug, which is now Mount Warning. The soils of dark basalt feed a rainforest of strangler figs, tree ferns, giant stinging trees and rare Antarctic beech, which clings on in the cool mountain mists as a relic of the ancient southern continent. Birds such as the Albert's lyrebird and the paradise riflebird live in the forest, and rivers cut through to waterfalls that pour over basalt cliffs.

The riding here is some of the best near any city in Australia. The roads of the hinterland, such as the climbs to Beechmont, Springbrook and Tamborine Mountain, are narrow, winding and well surfaced, with tight bends, hairpins and views down to the coast, and they are popular with riders at the weekend. Police patrols and speed cameras are common, and wet leaves and gravel can make corners treacherous after rain. Early morning rides, before the tourists arrive, are the most pleasant, with mist rising from the valleys. Summer brings heavy storms and humidity, while autumn and spring are mild.

The nearest places, Tallebudgera Valley, Bonogin and Lower Beechmont, are suburban and rural communities, with a few shops, cafes and fuel stations, and the Gold Coast itself, only a short ride away, has every service. Stop at a hinterland bakery for a pie, an Australian institution, and a flat white. Take care with wildlife on the road at dawn and dusk, particularly wallabies and kangaroos, which can appear suddenly.
t.mount warning national park@-28.4,153.3:
Wollumbin, as the Bundjalung people call it, rises on the Queensland border like a huge broken tooth, the central plug of the eroded Tweed volcano. Captain Cook saw it from the sea in 1770 and named it Mount Warning, as a signal of the dangerous reefs offshore. At just over eleven hundred metres it is not high, but standing alone above a vast bowl, ringed by the cliffs of the old crater rim, it looks far greater. It is often said to be the first place on the Australian mainland to catch the sun each morning, though that depends on how you measure.

For the Bundjalung, Wollumbin is a sacred place, a site of law and ceremony, and elders have asked visitors not to climb it. The summit track, a steep climb of several hours that was once one of the most popular walks in the country, has been closed for long periods in recent years, so check the current status before planning anything, and respect whatever the position is. The mountain can be admired from many places around the valley, and the old crater rim has lovely drives of its own.

The park protects a mix of rainforest, eucalypt forest and heath, and it belongs to the Gondwana Rainforests group inscribed by UNESCO. Rainforest here is rich with ferns, orchids, vines and huge fig trees, and the creeks run clear over basalt boulders. Mist often wraps the summit in the early morning, and the lowland valley beneath is a patchwork of sugar cane, banana farms and green paddocks.

Riding in the Tweed valley is a delight. The road to the base of the mountain winds up from Murwillumbah through farmland, and the loop around the crater rim, over the ranges to Nimbin and the Nightcap, is a favourite with local riders: smooth tarmac, plenty of bends, and views over the caldera. Nimbin itself, a small town known since the 1973 Aquarius Festival for its alternative lifestyle, is a colourful place to stop for coffee, though it is well known for other things too, so keep your wits about you. Watch for logging trucks, cattle on the road and wet conditions after rain.

Murwillumbah has fuel, cafes, and an excellent art gallery, and is the sensible place to fill up before heading into the hills. Summer, from December to March, brings storms and floods, and the roads can be closed by landslides, so look at the weather forecast and the latest road reports before setting out.
t.site of memphis@29.9,31.3:
Memphis was the first capital of a unified Egypt, or so tradition says, and for much of the Old Kingdom it was the centre of the world's most ordered state. Today there is little of it to see, because the city was built of mud brick and stripped for stone, and the Nile shifted away. What remains is a quiet area of palm groves and fields near the village of Mit Rahina, south of Cairo, where an open-air museum shows a few fragments of the capital that once stretched for kilometres along the river.

The best-known piece is the colossal statue of Ramesses II, carved in limestone and lying on its back under a roof, so that you look down at it from a gallery. It is a calm, almost human face, with a half smile, and it is one of the finest pieces of Egyptian sculpture outside a major museum. A large alabaster sphinx sits nearby, and there are stelae, columns and fragments from the temple of Ptah, the god of craftsmen and the patron deity of the city, from whom, by a long road of linguistic change, the name of Egypt is said to derive.

Memphis is part of a larger World Heritage area, listed in 1979, that includes the pyramid fields stretching from Giza to Dahshur, with Saqqara and its Step Pyramid a short way to the west. The city was the living side of the necropolis, and the two go together. Visitors usually combine the sites in a day, and on a motorbike you can do that with a little patience.

Riding in the Cairo area demands attention. Traffic is dense and apparently improvised, speed bumps appear without warning, lanes are a suggestion, and the dust and heat are constant. Drive defensively, avoid night riding, and keep your documents handy at checkpoints. The roads along the canals and between the palm groves south of the city are quieter, with a rural rhythm of donkey carts and children on bicycles, and they are a pleasure early in the morning.

Helwan, a city of several hundred thousand people about four kilometres away, has fuel, food and shops. Egyptian street food is excellent and cheap: koshari, falafel and fresh bread, with sweet tea at every stop. Carry plenty of water and avoid the midday heat in summer.

The ride links Memphis with the Mosque of Ibn Tulun in Cairo, a ninth-century monument of calm brick and stucco.
t.joliet@41.5,-88.1:
Joliet is not pretty and does not pretend to be, which is exactly why it makes a good Route 66 stop. The old state penitentiary, a huge, castle-like fortress in local limestone that opened in the middle of the nineteenth century, was closed in 2002 and is now partly open for tours, and film fans will recognise it from the opening of The Blues Brothers. The Rialto Square Theatre, built in 1926, is something else entirely, a gorgeous, over-the-top movie palace in Beaux-Arts style with chandeliers, marble and a ceiling worthy of a cathedral. Together they give you a fair summary of the town: tough and ornate in the same breath.

Traffic can be heavy on weekdays and the surfaces patchy, with frost damage from winters that come hard in northern Illinois. It is best taken as a gentle warm-up before the quieter, flatter country of the prairie to the south. Fuel and food are everywhere, with a large population of nearly a hundred and fifty thousand, so this is the place to prepare, grab breakfast and decide how many miles you really want to cover. Early spring and autumn are comfortable; summer humidity can be heavy.
t.pontiac@40.9,-88.6:
Pontiac, Illinois, is a courthouse town of around twelve thousand people on the Vermilion River, and for anyone with a soft spot for Route 66 it is something close to a pilgrimage. The county courthouse and its square are the centre of the place, and the town has the unhurried feel of somewhere that knows who it is. The Vermilion River loops through the middle, and there is a small park beside it with a path along the bank.

A museum in an old firehouse houses an Illinois Route 66 Hall of Fame, with memorabilia, photographs and vintage signs collected from along the road, and nearby there is a museum of classic cars and one of the town's own history. Spring and autumn are the best times, when the air is clear and the corn is either low and green or golden and dry. Pontiac has stations and a few cafes for food, so fill up and have lunch here. t.mount glorious@-27.3,152.8:
Mount Glorious is the high point of a good day out of Brisbane, a small settlement strung along the crest of the D'Aguilar Range where the air is noticeably cooler and the forest is rainforest rather than bushland. Brisbane's riders have used this road for generations, and on a weekend morning you will see bikes parked outside the cafe on the summit in numbers that suggest a quiet agreement among the locals about where to be.

The surface has patches and the occasional fallen branch after storms, so ride it like a road, not a circuit. Descending on the other side towards Wivenhoe Dam, the road opens up a little, and you can see the lake that supplies much of south-east Queensland.

What is interesting here is how different the world is at height. Cloud forest, tree ferns, the sound of whipbirds and the smell of wet leaves, all within a short ride of a city of two million. The national parks around Mount Glorious are protected for good reason, and there are short walking tracks if you want to break up the riding. Wildlife is a hazard as much as a pleasure, with wallabies and birds at dawn and dusk, which is another reason to avoid pushing too hard.

Fuel is not up here, so top up before the climb. Samford Valley and Ferny Grove, the larger suburbs on the Brisbane side, are the places to do it, and the cafe at the top is the thing to look forward to. Ride it early on a clear day in the cooler months, between about April and October, and you will understand why people come back week after week.
t.la grange@42.7,-88.5:
La Grange sits in a landscape that was made by ice, and the clearest way to read it is to look at the shape of the land. The Kettle Moraine, a long band of hills and hollows running through eastern Wisconsin, was built by the edge of the last ice sheet, which dropped its load of gravel, sand and boulders as it melted. Kettles are the round hollows left when buried blocks of ice melted, and kames and eskers are the mounds and ridges of gravel that the meltwater left behind. Together they give the countryside a rolling, tumbled feel, with no straight lines anywhere.

The town of La Grange itself is small and rural, a patchwork of farms, woods and lakes, and Elkhorn, the county seat, is a short distance away. The countryside is at its most striking in October, when the oaks turn rust-red and the maples blaze orange.

The roads that cross the moraine are superb for riding. They climb and fall over the hills in a chain of easy bends, with good surfaces, quiet traffic and views over woods and farms from the ridges. A marked scenic drive links many of the best stretches, and on a fine weekend it attracts a lot of riders and cyclists, so you may find yourself in good company. The corners are not tight, but they are constant, and the combination of rhythm and scenery makes for a very relaxing ride. Watch for deer at dawn and dusk, and for gravel at the edges of the farm entrances.

Elkhorn, six kilometres away, has fuel and cafes, and East Troy, ten kilometres off, has a lovely old square and a few places to eat. La Grange itself has little in the way of services, so plan your stops. The roads are open year-round, but winter brings ice and snow, and the best time to ride is from May to October. Summer is warm and humid, with thunderstorms in the afternoons, so carry waterproofs and watch the sky.
t.eagle@42.8,-88.5:

t.kirovsk@67.6,33.7:

t.pre hispanic town of uxmal@20.4,-89.8:

t.uxmal@20.4,-89.8:

t.kem@65.0,34.6:

t.umba@66.7,34.3:

t.wadi al hitan@29.3,30.2:

t.kandalaksha@67.2,32.4:

t.olenegorsk@68.1,33.3:

t.zapolyarny@69.4,30.8:
Zapolyarny means beyond the polar circle, and the town does not apologize for the name. The nickel works in the area are among the largest in the north, and the sulfur from the smelters has left the surrounding hills stripped of trees, a scar that is visible for miles.

The Kola Superdeep Borehole, drilled by Soviet scientists from 1970 and reaching more than twelve kilometers by 1989, is the deepest artificial point on earth. It lies a short distance from town, and the site is now abandoned, with a rusted, welded cap over the shaft and a ruined research building. The project never reached its target and was closed in the 1990s, but it taught geologists a great deal about the crust, including the surprise of finding water far deeper than expected.

Pechenga Monastery, founded in the sixteenth century by the monk Tryphon, was once the northernmost in the world, and the settlement of Pechenga lies about eighteen kilometers away. Fuel stations and supermarkets are available in the town, and it is the best place to stock up before heading to the coast. Distances are long, and services beyond are scarce. At midnight in July, the light is low and golden across the tundra, and the whole landscape looks like a painting.
t.titovka@69.5,32.0:
Titovka is barely a place at all on the map, just a bridge over a fast, rocky river on the road between Murmansk and the Norwegian border, a few buildings and a roadside stop. But anyone heading for the Sredny and Rybachy peninsulas knows the name, because this is where the rough track north leaves the paved road. It is not a place for carelessness: unexploded ordnance has been found here for decades, so keep to tracks and paths.

The road from Murmansk to Titovka is paved, with long straights and sweeping bends across a rolling landscape of low hills, lakes and dwarf birch, and the views open wide in every direction. Beyond, the track north to Sredny is unpaved, rough and in places deeply rutted, with water crossings after rain. It is best tackled on a light adventure bike with good tyres and some experience off road. Weather changes fast this far north; even in July, a sunny morning can turn to cold rain and fog within an hour.

Practical matters need real planning. The nearest town on the map, Zaozyorsk, is a closed naval town and not open to casual visitors, so fill up in Murmansk or Zapolyarny and carry extra fuel if you plan to explore the peninsulas. The peninsulas lie in a border zone, so check the current permit rules before you go. Bring warm, waterproof clothing, food and water, and treat the roadside stop at Titovka as a last outpost of comfort before the tundra takes over.
t.sredny peninsula@69.7,32.1:
Sredny means middle, and the name is exact: this peninsula sits between the mainland of the Kola coast and the larger Rybachy Peninsula, joined to both by narrow isthmuses, a low, treeless stretch of tundra, rock and lakes pushed out into the Barents Sea. It looks empty, and it mostly is, but it has a long human history. Pomor fishermen from the White Sea worked these coasts for centuries, and between the world wars the western part belonged to Finland, as part of the narrow corridor that gave the Finns access to the Arctic Ocean.

The Second World War left the deepest marks. In 1941 the German advance toward Murmansk was stopped on the ridge at the southern neck of Sredny, and the front froze there for three years. Soviet troops held the peninsulas throughout the war, supplied by sea under constant attack, and the ground is still littered with trenches, gun positions, barbed wire and the debris of war. Later came the Cold War: garrisons, airstrips and radar posts, most of them abandoned in the 1990s and now crumbling slowly in the wind.

The riding is serious off-road work. There is no paved road on the peninsula, only tracks of gravel, sand, rock and mud that braid across the tundra and split into multiple ruts where vehicles have avoided the worst sections. Some fords can be deep after heavy rain or snowmelt, and the ground near lakes and streams can be boggy. A light adventure bike with knobbly tyres, riding in company, is the right approach. In summer the sun never sets, which helps, but fog can roll in from the sea at any time and turn a clear day grey and cold within minutes.

You are a long way from help here. Zaozyorsk, the nearest town on the map, is a closed naval settlement, so bring all the fuel, food and water you will need from Murmansk or Zapolyarny. The peninsula lies inside the border zone, and permits have been required in the past, so check before you go. In return you get an almost completely wild Arctic coast, wildflowers in July, reindeer and Arctic terns, and a sense of space that few places in Europe can match.
t.rybachy peninsula@69.7,32.6:
At the end of the track, past the ruined garrisons of Sredny and across another narrow neck of land, lies Rybachy, the Fishermen's Peninsula, the northernmost reach of mainland European Russia. Its tip, Cape Nemetsky, has a lighthouse and a view north to nothing but the open Barents Sea. The name is old: Russian Pomors and Norwegian fishermen worked these waters for cod and halibut for centuries, salting their catch in seasonal camps along the shore, and fishing villages survived here until the Soviet period swept them away.

The landscape is dramatic in an understated way. The peninsula is a plateau of layered sandstone and slate, tilted and broken into cliffs along the coast, with tundra on top and streams cutting down to the sea. There are waterfalls tumbling over coastal cliffs, beaches of pebbles and driftwood, and small lakes full of trout. In summer the tundra blooms with cloudberries, cotton grass and tiny Arctic flowers, and the sea birds nest on the cliffs. The light is the great thing here: soft and endless in June and July, low and golden in August.

Getting around is hard work. The tracks across Rybachy are rough, rocky and often muddy, with fords, deep ruts and sections where the trail disappears into a confusion of options. A light, capable bike, good tyres, spare parts and a riding partner are essential, and a GPS track is very helpful. The weather can be brutal even in summer, with gale-force winds, cold rain and fog off the sea, and conditions can change within an hour. Take warm layers and full waterproofs regardless of the forecast.

There are no services on the peninsula, apart from a few seasonal tourist camps that may or may not be operating. Carry all fuel, food and water for the round trip from Murmansk or Zapolyarny, and remember that Zaozyorsk is a closed town. The area is a border zone, so check permit requirements well ahead. People who make it out here tend to talk about it for years afterwards: the cliffs, the wind, the light, and the sense of having reached the very edge of the continent.
t.mustatunturi@69.6,31.8:
The name is Finnish, Musta-Tunturi, the Black Fell, and it refers to the long, dark ridge of rock that rises across the neck of land joining the Sredny Peninsula to the mainland. In the summer of 1941 the German mountain troops advancing on Murmansk were stopped here, and for the next three years, until the Soviet offensive of October 1944, the front line ran along this ridge. Soldiers on both sides lived in dugouts blasted out of rock, in temperatures far below freezing and in months of darkness, often within shouting distance of each other.

Today the ridge carries a memorial complex and the remains of the positions are everywhere: trenches cut into stone, collapsed bunkers, rusting wire, shell fragments and sometimes bones. The Russian phrase associated with this place is about the enemy not passing, and the defence of the peninsulas is remembered as one of the epics of the Arctic war. Visitors leave flowers and small tokens at the monuments. It is a sombre place, and the silence of the tundra around it makes the history feel close.

The ride here, as the finish of a loop out to the peninsulas, comes on rough tracks over the tundra, with the ridge looming ahead and the sea visible on both sides. The tracks are rocky, rutted and sometimes muddy, with steep, loose sections where the trail climbs over the ridge and fords where streams cross. In wet weather the slopes can be slippery, and fog can hide the way. The views from the top, when it is clear, take in the Barents Sea, the bays and the empty hills rolling away toward Norway.

There is nothing here in the way of services. Bring fuel, food and water from Murmansk or Zapolyarny, and do not count on Zaozyorsk, which is a closed military town. Keep to existing tracks and paths, because unexploded munitions are still found in the area. Take the time to walk among the positions and think about what it meant to hold this ridge through three Arctic winters. It is one of the most moving places in the far north, and the right note to end a ride on.
